title: Creativity
authors: Guilford, J. P.
key_findings: APA presidential address (American Psychologist 5(9):444-454) credited with starting psychological creativity research; Guilford's later Structure-of-Intellect model separates divergent from convergent production.
practical_applications: Separate a 'generate many' phase from a 'pick one' phase.
limitations: Known through secondary sources only; full text not read.

title: Divergent Thinking as an Indicator of Creative Potential
authors: Runco, M. A.; Acar, S.
key_findings: Divergent-thinking (DT) tests estimate creative potential, not achievement; DT is not the same as creative thinking; tests are reliable and moderately predictive, 'far from perfect'.
practical_applications: Many ideas is a means, not the goal: judge final work on originality + fit, not idea count.
limitations: Abstract/excerpts only; later papers flag psychometric problems of DT scores.

title: The associative basis of the creative process
authors: Mednick, S. A.
key_findings: Creativity = combining associative elements into new useful combinations; the more remote the elements, the more creative; proposed flatter associative hierarchies in creative people (basis of the Remote Associates Test).
Benedek & Neubauer (2013, PMC3924568) found hierarchies did not differ, but creative people showed higher associative fluency and more uncommon responses.
practical_applications: Deliberately pair distant domains (eyewear x temple fair, glasses x weather) to push past first associations.
limitations: No abstract; content via secondary sources; core hierarchy hypothesis only partly supported.

title: Analogical problem solving
authors: Gick, M. L.; Holyoak, K. J.
key_findings: People who read a military story often transferred its solution to Duncker's radiation problem only when hinted; without a hint analogous solutions dropped markedly; Gick & Holyoak 1983: two analogues improve transfer (schema induction).
practical_applications: Analogies do not arrive by themselves: explicitly ask 'what else works like this?' and give 2+ source examples from different domains.
limitations: Abstract and secondary summaries; exact transfer rates not captured.

title: Conceptual Integration Networks
authors: Fauconnier, G.; Turner, M.
key_findings: Blending is a general cognitive operation: two input spaces, a generic space and a blended space with emergent structure; network types simplex, mirror, single-scope, double-scope. Cognitive Science 22(2):133-187.
practical_applications: Visual metaphors (lens = window, frame = character) as deliberate blends; check the blend's emergent meaning reads clearly.
limitations: Secondary summaries only; theory, little predictive experimental test.

title: Productivity Loss in Brainstorming Groups: Toward the Solution of a Riddle
authors: Diehl, M.; Stroebe, W.
key_findings: Four experiments: production blocking (waiting to speak) accounted for most of the productivity loss of interactive vs nominal groups; free riding and evaluation apprehension were minor.
practical_applications: Generate alone first, then pool (nominal group / brainwriting).
limitations: Abstract/secondary only; lab tasks, students.

title: Productivity Loss in Brainstorming Groups: A Meta-Analytic Integration
authors: Mullen, B.; Johnson, C.; Salas, E.
key_findings: Interactive brainstorming groups produce fewer and lower-quality ideas than nominal groups; losses grow with group size, experimenter presence and spoken (vs written) ideas.
practical_applications: Classic 'everyone shout ideas' brainstorming is the weakest format; write ideas individually.
limitations: Abstract only; Diehl & Stroebe disputed some mechanism conclusions.

title: Idea Generation in Groups: A Basis for Creativity in Organizations
authors: Paulus, P. B.; Yang, H.-C.
key_findings: In a brainwriting paradigm (writing ideas on slips and passing them on), idea-sharing groups outperformed nominal groups both during the session and in a later individual session.
practical_applications: Brainwriting style: read others' written ideas, then extend silently - works for Claude-vs-user idea exchange too.
limitations: Abstract only; Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 82(1):76-87.

title: Idea Generation and the Quality of the Best Idea
authors: Girotra, K.; Terwiesch, C.; Ulrich, K. T.
key_findings: Hybrid structure (work alone, then pool and evaluate as a team) beat team-only on number of ideas, quality, and ability to discern the best idea; building on others' ideas did not yield more or better ideas.
Best-idea quality depends on mean quality, number, variance, and selection ability.
practical_applications: We need the best idea, not the average: maximise variance in generation, then select carefully with criteria.
limitations: Abstract only; lab product-idea task.

title: Productivity is not enough: A comparison of interactive and nominal groups on idea generation and selection
authors: Rietzschel, E. F.; Nijstad, B. A.; Stroebe, W.
key_findings: J. Exp. Soc. Psych. 42:244-251. Related dissertation abstract: productivity was not related to the quality of selected ideas; a 2009 article by the same authors says using the right selection criteria is essential.
practical_applications: Selection is a separate skill: score ideas against explicit criteria, otherwise people pick the safe/feasible one.
limitations: Bibliographic only; finding linked to this paper via related abstracts.

title: Does Incubation Enhance Problem Solving? A Meta-Analytic Review
authors: Sio, U. N.; Ormerod, T. C.
key_findings: 117 studies, positive incubation effect (mean d about 0.29 per Gilhooly 2016).
Longer preparation -> larger effect; high-demand filler tasks -> smaller; low-demand tasks beat rest for linguistic insight problems; effects differ by problem type.
practical_applications: Work the brief hard first, then switch to a low-demand task and come back before final selection.
limitations: Abstract and secondary summaries; lab puzzles.

title: Creativity and Innovation Under Constraints: A Cross-Disciplinary Integrative Review
authors: Acar, O. A.; Tarakci, M.; van Knippenberg, D.
key_findings: Constraint research across management fields is fragmented with conflicting findings; builds a taxonomy of constraints and mediating mechanisms (motivation, cognition, social context).
practical_applications: Constraints are not automatically good or bad; pick constraints that force search away from defaults (e.g., 'no coffee shop, no sunset').
limitations: Abstract only; taxonomy categories not verified; the common 'inverted-U' summary was not confirmed this session.

title: The Effectiveness of Creativity Training: A Quantitative Review
authors: Scott, G.; Leritz, L. E.; Mumford, M. D.
key_findings: 70 studies; well-designed creativity training typically yields gains that generalise across criteria; programmes focused on cognitive skills and heuristics did better.
practical_applications: Heuristic-based methods (problem finding, combination, idea evaluation) are the trainable core.
limitations: Abstract/secondary; see SioLortieForgues2024 on publication bias.

title: Creativity Enhancement Methods for Adults: A Meta-Analysis
authors: Haase, J.; Hanel, P. H. P.; Gronau, N.
key_findings: 332 effect sizes, 12 method categories, overall g = 0.53; complex training courses, meditation and cultural exposure strongest (g = 0.66); drugs g = 0.10 n.s.; reported no publication bias.
practical_applications: Exposure to varied culture/references is a legitimate input step (moodboards from different eras/countries).
limitations: Abstract only; publication-bias conclusion contradicted by SioLortieForgues2024.

title: The Impact of Creativity Training on Creative Performance
authors: Sio, U. N.; Lortie-Forgues, H.
key_findings: 169 studies (844 effect sizes, 48 unpublished); unadjusted 0.53 SD; converging evidence of strong publication bias, adjusted estimates 0.29-0.32 SD; many methodological shortcomings, little improvement over time.
practical_applications: Expect modest gains from any named creativity method; don't promise big effects.
limitations: Abstract/preprint summary only.

title: Thinking hats and good men: Structured techniques in a problem construction task
authors: Vernon, D.; Hocking, I.
key_findings: Six hats and 'six men' (5W1H) both improved fluency and originality in problem construction vs controls; published abstract and preprint disagree on which technique had the more robust effect.
Authors' 2016 follow-ups: order of hats had no effect (possibly underpowered); a placebo-controlled study found active techniques beat placebo.
practical_applications: Six hats is acceptable as a perspective-switching prompt, but evidence is a handful of small studies; 5W1H questions work about as well.
limitations: Small samples, one lab; search summaries only; no large independent trial found.

title: Experimental assessment of TRIZ effectiveness in idea generation (J. Mechanical Design version: TRIZ ideation effectiveness study)
authors: Vargas Hernandez, N.; Schmidt, L. C.; Okudan Kremer, G. E.
key_findings: TRIZ improved novelty and variety but slightly reduced quantity vs ad-hoc ideation; conference version: method fit depends on the outcome sought.
practical_applications: TRIZ suits engineering contradictions (lens thin AND strong); limited relevance to story ideation.
limitations: Search summary only; engineering students; exact JMD title not captured.

title: General morphological analysis as a basic scientific modelling method
authors: Ritchey, T.
key_findings: GMA (extending Zwicky) structures a problem space ('morphospace') into parameters and values, then synthesises solutions by combining values and removing inconsistent pairs (Technological Forecasting and Social Change 126:81-91).
practical_applications: Story matrix: setting x conflict x glasses role x ending -> forced distinct combinations.
limitations: Method description by its main proponent; no controlled efficacy evidence found.

title: Doing Design Thinking: Conceptual Review, Synthesis, and Research Agenda
authors: Micheli, P.; et al.
key_findings: Systematic review + card sort with designers: 10 attributes and 8 tools of design thinking; substantial disagreement between promoters and critics on attributes, applicability and outcomes.
A later paper reports the reviewed literature is 15% conceptual, 38% anecdotal, 44% qualitative (secondary).
practical_applications: Use design-thinking tools (user empathy, prototyping, iteration) as craft, not as a proven method.
limitations: Abstract and secondary summaries only.

title: Design Thinking: Critical Analysis and Future Evolution
authors: Verganti, R.; Dell'Era, C.; Swan, K. S.
key_findings: JPIM editorial summarising critiques: design-thinking studies judged empirically unconvincing and theoretically disconnected from innovation-management theory.
practical_applications: Do not cite 'design thinking' as evidence that an idea works.
limitations: Search summary only.

title: Parallel Prototyping Leads to Better Design Results, More Divergence, and Increased Self-Efficacy
authors: Dow, S. P.; Glassco, A.; Kass, J.; Schwarz, M.; Schwartz, D. L.; Klemmer, S. R.
key_findings: Novices designing web ads: parallel prototyping beat serial on all performance measures, produced more diverse prototypes (independent raters), increased self-efficacy, and more positive reactions to critique.
Murphy et al. 2022 reports similar advantages in engineering design.
practical_applications: Make 3 rough directions side by side before polishing one; compare, then iterate the winner.
limitations: Abstract/summaries only; novice sample; one task type.

title: Design fixation
authors: Jansson, D. G.; Smith, S. M.
key_findings: Showing an example solution made designers (incl. professionals) repeat its features, even flawed ones; instructions to avoid the features did not reduce fixation.
Mixed later evidence: Purcell et al. 1993 replications largely unsuccessful, effects tied to familiarity; Chrysikou & Weisberg found defixation instructions helped.
practical_applications: Reference images and AI drafts anchor us; generate own directions before looking at references or AI output.
limitations: Known via secondary papers (Design Studies); replication mixed - medium confidence.

title: Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content
authors: Doshi, A. R.; Hauser, O. P.
key_findings: 293 writers, 600 evaluators; conditions 0, 1 or 5 GPT-4 ideas. Novelty +5.4% (1 idea) and +8.1% (5 ideas); usefulness +3.7% / +9.0%.
Gains largest for less creative writers (novelty up to +10.7%), roughly equalising them with more creative writers.
Stories became more similar to each other (+10.7% / +8.9% of similarity range) and about 5% more similar to the AI ideas - a social dilemma: individuals better off, collective diversity down.
practical_applications: AI ideas raise the floor but pull everyone toward the same stories: use AI for volume/critique, but force divergence (different seeds, constraints, human-first idea) and check against our own past output.
limitations: 8-sentence stories, one LLM, no interaction with the model, UK online sample, opt-in idea use.

title: Homogenization Effects of Large Language Models on Human Creative Ideation
authors: Anderson, B. R.; Shah, J. H.; Kreminski, M.
key_findings: 36 participants, four TTCT-style divergent tasks: different users produced less semantically distinct ideas with ChatGPT than with a non-AI creativity support tool (ACM Creativity & Cognition 2024).
practical_applications: Same model + similar prompt = similar ideas across users; vary the input, not just ask again.
limitations: Small sample; abstract only.

title: Prompting Diverse Ideas: Increasing AI Idea Variance
authors: Meincke, L.; Mollick, E.; Terwiesch, C.
key_findings: GPT-4 with minimal prompting produced less diverse idea pools than groups of humans; personas and creativity-technique prompts helped somewhat; chain-of-thought prompting gave the highest diversity, close to human groups.
Authors suggest using multiple models to add variety.
practical_applications: Ask the model to first list many distinct concepts briefly, then develop each; mix models (Claude/Codex/FLUX) and seeds.
limitations: Working paper (SSRN/arXiv); diversity measured by embeddings, not by audience response; product-idea domain.
